A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. 333 ``` 334 335 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 336 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 337 animation: none; 338 z-index: 100; 339 } 340 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 341 display: none; 342 } 343 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 344 animation: none; 345 } 346 ``` 347 348 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update. 416 417 If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 418 419 ## Next steps 420 421 You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. The enter fade is slower (210ms) and delayed until the exit completes, while its slide movement runs longer (400ms): 171 172 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 173 :root { 174 --duration-exit: 150ms; 175 --duration-enter: 210ms; 176 --duration-move: 400ms; 177 } 178 179 ::view-transition-old(.slide-down) { 180 animation: 181 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both fade reverse, 182 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both slide-y reverse; 183 } 184 ::view-transition-new(.slide-up) { 185 animation: 186 var(--duration-enter) ease-in var(--duration-exit) both fade, 187 var(--duration-move) ease-in both slide-y; 188 } 189 190 @keyframes fade { 191 from { 192 filter: blur(3px); 193 opacity: 0; 194 } 195 to { 196 filter: blur(0); 197 opacity: 1; 198 } 199 } 200 @keyframes slide-y { 201 from { 202 transform: translateY(10px); 203 } 204 to { 205 transform: translateY(0); 206 } 207 } 208 ``` 209 210 The asymmetry is deliberate. Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it. The `var(--duration-exit)` delay on the enter fade means the new content waits for the old content to finish leaving before it becomes visible. 211 212 If we refresh the page, the skeleton slides down and fades out, and a moment later the real content slides up and fades in. 213 214 ### Step 3: Add directional motion for navigation 215 216 The gallery now has morphing images and animated loading states. But navigating between pages still has no directional signal. Forward and back navigations look identical. The user cannot tell from the animation whether they moved deeper into the app or returned to a previous page. 217 218 In film and animation, horizontal direction encodes spatial position. Moving left means progressing forward (like turning a page in a left-to-right language). Moving right means going back. This convention is so ingrained that violating it feels disorienting. 219 220 Use the `transitionTypes` prop on `` to tag forward navigations: 221 222 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 223 224 {/* photo thumbnail */} 225 226 ``` 227 228 The same pattern works for any navigation within the app. For example, previous/next arrows on a photo detail page can use `nav-back` and `nav-forward` to animate in the corresponding direction. 229 230 For links that return the user to a previous page, use `nav-back`: 231 232 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 233 234 ← Gallery 235 236 ``` 237 238 The transition type is not automatic. You decide which links are "forward" and which are "back" based on your app's navigation hierarchy. 239 240 Then wrap page content in a `ViewTransition` that maps transition types to directional animations: 241 242 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 243 256 {/* page content */} 257 258 ``` 259 260 The `enter` and `exit` props accept an object keyed by transition type. When a navigation carries the `nav-forward` type, the exit animation slides old content left and the enter animation slides new content in from the right. The `default: "none"` ensures that transitions without a type (browser back/forward, `router.refresh()`, Suspense reveals) produce no directional animation. 261 262 Wrap every participating page the same way. For the gallery to slide out on forward navigation and back in on `nav-back`, its page needs the same wrapper. Put the wrapper in each `page.tsx`, not the layout. Layouts persist across navigations, so enter and exit never fire there: 263 264 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 265 278 279 280 ``` 281 282 The CSS for directional slides: 283 284 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 285 ::view-transition-old(.nav-forward) { 286 --slide-offset: -60px; 287 animation: 288 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 289 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 290 } 291 ::view-transition-new(.nav-forward) { 292 --slide-offset: 60px; 293 animation: 294 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 295 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 296 } 297 298 ::view-transition-old(.nav-back) { 299 --slide-offset: 60px; 300 animation: 301 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 302 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 303 } 304 ::view-transition-new(.nav-back) { 305 --slide-offset: -60px; 306 animation: 307 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 308 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 309 } 310 311 @keyframes slide { 312 from { 313 translate: var(--slide-offset); 314 } 315 to { 316 translate: 0; 317 } 318 } 319 ``` 320 321 The 60px offset is enough to communicate direction without making the user track a fast-moving element across the screen. 322 323 #### Anchoring the header 324 325 During directional slides, the header should not move. A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 326 327 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 328 329 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 330
331 {/* navigation links */} 332
333 ``` 334 335 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 336 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 337 animation: none; 338 z-index: 100; 339 } 340 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 341 display: none; 342 } 343 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 344 animation: none; 345 } 346 ``` 347 348 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content. 349 350 If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 351 352 Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props. 353 354 #### Keeping the page interactive 355 356 While a transition runs, the `::view-transition` overlay captures pointer events, so clicks during the animation are lost. Let them pass through to the live page: 357 358 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 359 ::view-transition { 360 pointer-events: none; 361 } 362 ``` 363 364 This restores interactivity for unnamed content. Hit-testing still skips named participants (like the anchored header) for the transition's duration, so keep transitions short and avoid naming elements the user clicks rapidly. 365 366 #### Respecting reduced motion 367 368 Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 369 370 The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 371 372 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 373 @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 374 ::view-transition-old(*), 375 ::view-transition-new(*), 376 ::view-transition-group(*) { 377 animation-duration: 0s !important; 378 animation-delay: 0s !important; 379 } 380 } 381 ``` 382 383 Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. A more refined approach would preserve crossfades and opacity transitions while removing positional movement. See ["No Motion Isn't Always prefers-reduced-motion"](https://css-tricks.com/nuking-motion-with-prefers-reduced-motion/) for more on this. 384 385 ### Step 4: Crossfade content within the same route 386 387 The gallery has a photographer section with tabs. Each tab shows a different photographer's photos, but the route structure is the same: `/collection/[slug]`. Clicking between tabs does not feel like navigating to a new page. It feels like switching content within the same container. 388 389 A directional slide would be wrong here. Slides communicate "going to a new place." A crossfade communicates "same place, different content." The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap). 390 391 Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. When the key changes, React triggers a transition between the old and new content: 392 393 ```tsx filename="app/collection/[slug]/page.tsx" 394 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 395 396 export default async function CollectionPage({ params }) { 397 const { slug } = await params 398 399 return ( 400 }> 401 408 409 410 411 ) 412 } 413 ``` 414 415 The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update. 416 417 If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 418 419 ## Next steps 420 421 You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. Shared elements communicate continuity across routes. Suspense reveals animate loading handoffs. Directional slides encode navigation history. events.content:
All four patterns are wired up. `AGENTS.md` pointed me at `node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/02-guides/view-transitions.md`, which turned out to be a complete guide for exactly this — I followed its recipes rather than my priors.

## What changed

**`types/react-canary.d.ts`** (new) — `ViewTransition` and `addTransitionType` live in `@types/react/canary.d.ts`, which isn't auto-included. A triple-slash reference enables it project-wide. (Runtime needs nothing: Next 16 aliases `react` to a bundled 19.3 canary that exports `ViewTransition` from both the client and `react-server` builds — I verified both, so it works in Server Components with no `'use client'`.)

**`app/ProductImage.tsx`** (new) — the shared-element morph. `name={`product-image-${slug}`}` with `share="morph"` + `default="none"`. Both call sites go through it so the names can't drift apart.

**`app/PageTransition.tsx`** (new) — the directional wrapper, mapping `nav-forward`/`nav-back` transition types to CSS classes with `default: 'none'`. Rendered in each `page.tsx`, not the layout, since layouts persist and would never fire enter/exit.

**`app/ProductGrid.tsx`** — `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}` on the cards, thumbnail swapped for `ProductImage`.

**`app/page.tsx` / `app/product/[slug]/page.tsx`** — `PageTransition` wrapper, `transitionTypes={['nav-back']}` on the back link, and Suspense reveals (`exit="slide-down"` on the fallback, `enter="slide-up"` on the content). The hero stays outside the Suspense boundary so it commits with the navigation and can pair with the thumbnail.

**`app/globals.css`** — morph/reveal/slide keyframes on shared duration tokens, `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }` so clicks aren't swallowed mid-animation, and the reduced-motion block.

## Two things worth knowing

**I changed the detail page's outer `<div>` to `<main>`.** It was the only page not using `main`, so it rendered with no padding or max-width while the grid sat in a centered 1200px container. The morph would have flown from inside that container to a full-bleed viewport edge — the feature looking broken. One line, but it does change that page's existing layout, so revert it if the full-bleed was intentional.

**Reduced motion goes slightly beyond the guide's suggestion.** Rather than zeroing every duration, I zero only group and image-pair durations — killing all positional and geometric movement — and keep a 120ms opacity-only crossfade, plus stilling the infinite skeleton pulse. The comment in the CSS says how to get a hard cut instead if you prefer.

## Verification

`tsc --noEmit` clean, `next build` clean. I confirmed in the served markup that the thumbnail and hero emit matching `vt-name`s, that `transitionTypes` stays in the RSC payload instead of leaking onto the `<a>`, that the detail Suspense boundary genuinely streams, and that all 12 `::view-transition-*` rules survive Turbopack's CSS pipeline (the `.morph` class-argument selectors were the risk).

I caught one real bug this way: with `<main>` outside the wrapper, the home page's `PageTransition` had two host children and SSR emitted `vt-name="page-gallery"` twice. Moving `<main>` inside makes both routes a single snapshot.

No browser is available in this sandbox, so I could not watch the animations actually play — the wiring and CSS are verified, the visual result is not.

Also: `next dev` regenerated `AGENTS.md` with its own expanded rules block (it says it does this by design), and `next build` added `.next/dev/types/**/*.ts` to `tsconfig.json` and created `next-env.d.ts`. Unrelated to my changes, but they're in your working tree. `.gitignore` doesn't cover `.next/`, `next-env.d.ts`, or `tsconfig.tsbuildinfo`, so those now show as untracked.
